title: The JavaScript Memory Model: GC, Leaks & Weak References
summary: Dense study-notes on how JavaScript manages memory: how garbage collection actually works inside the engine, the leak patterns that bite real apps, the WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef family, and how to hunt leaks with heap snapshots in DevTools.

chapters.title: Memory Fundamentals: Stack, Heap & References
points: Memory lifecycle in JS: allocate → use → release; the first two are your code, the third is the engine's GC
Stack vs heap: primitives and call frames live on the fast, fixed-size stack; objects, arrays, functions and closures live on the heap
Primitives copy by value, objects copy by reference — two variables can point at one heap object
const locks the binding, not the value: a const object's properties can still mutate
Closures capture variables by reference, so an escaping function keeps its captured scope on the heap
Shallow vs deep: spread and Object.assign copy one level; nested objects stay shared with the original
Strings are immutable — every concatenation allocates a new string and strands the old one for GC
Boxed wrappers (new String(5), new Number()) create pointless heap objects — use primitives
Hidden classes (V8): objects with the same shape share maps, cutting per-object overhead — shape churn costs memory
Allocation itself is cheap; the bill arrives at collection time, so allocation patterns shape GC behavior
Key definition: an object is garbage the moment nothing can reach it — references are the unit of lifetime
Mental picture (diagram): variable → reference → object on the heap; freeing means removing the arrow, not the box

chapters.title: Reachability & Mark-and-Sweep
points: Core rule: GC collects objects unreachable from the root set — lifetime = reachability
The roots: global object, current call stack, active module state, and anything the engine pins (e.g. DOM of a live document)
Mark-and-sweep phase 1 (mark): walk every edge from the roots, flag everything reachable
Phase 2 (sweep): everything unflagged is garbage; the engine reclaims its memory
Reachability is transitive — a live object keeps its entire reference subgraph alive
Cycles are fine: two objects referencing each other but unreachable from roots still get collected — this is why JS dropped pure reference counting
Unreachable ≠ freed instantly: collection timing is the engine's call, not yours
Retention: one stray reference to a big object can pin megabytes of subgraph — leaks are about edges, not object size
No destructors in JS: you can't run code 'when an object dies' (FinalizationRegistry is the one, unreliable exception)
Trace-based GC vs reference counting: tracing tolerates cycles; refcounting pays an increment/decrement on every assignment
Diagram: roots → live graph, plus a floating island of garbage no root points to
Litmus test: setting obj = null frees nothing while another variable still references the object

chapters.title: Under the Hood: V8's Generational GC
points: Generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so the heap is split into a young space and an old space
Minor GC (Scavenger in V8): a fast, semi-space copying collector that cleans the nursery and promotes survivors to old space
Major GC: mark-sweep/mark-compact over old space — slower, triggered by allocation pressure or promotion
Write barriers: old→young pointers are recorded so minor GC scans a small remembered set instead of the whole old heap
Incremental marking: the big mark phase is chopped into small steps interleaved with your JS to cap pause length
Concurrent + parallel phases: background and helper threads do marking/sweeping so the main thread mostly stops only briefly
Result: GC happens in short bursts at engine-chosen moments — never assume 'between frames' or 'when idle'
Hidden classes and pointer compression shrink per-object overhead — stable object shapes are GC-friendly too
You can't schedule GC in production: no exposed API — allocate less instead of 'forcing' collection
Dev-only escape hatch: run Chrome/Node with --expose-gc to call gc() in tests and benchmarks
Symptoms of memory pressure: rising heapUsed baseline, growing jank from more frequent GC, eventual OOM crash
Rule of thumb: tuning GC is off-limits; shaping allocation (fewer, smaller, shorter-lived objects) is your lever

chapters.title: Leak Pattern Clinic I: Timers, Listeners & Closures
points: Leak #1 — forgotten timers: a setInterval never cleared keeps its callback, its closure, and everything they capture, forever
Typical shape: mount() starts an interval, unmount() never calls clearInterval — one accumulates per re-mount
Leak #2 — listeners: addEventListener on a long-lived node (window, document) keeps the handler closure alive after its owner is 'gone'
removeEventListener needs the same function reference — anonymous handlers can never be removed
Modern fix: AbortController + addEventListener(type, fn, { signal }) — one abort() tears down every listener
Leak #3 — closures over big data: a tiny exported function can pin megabytes through its captured scope
Capture granularity: in V8 a variable survives if any closure in the same scope reads it — unrelated big locals can get pinned
Recreate-handler bug: passing a new arrow each render means old ones are never removed even if you 'remove' with the new ref
Pending timers from debounce/throttle hold their captured state — cancel them on teardown
Never-settling promises: awaiting closures that never resolve accumulate with everything they captured
Contract to memorize: every subscription (timer, listener, observer) needs a symmetric unsubscribe path
Code sketch: leaked interval vs fixed version with clearInterval in the cleanup function

chapters.title: Leak Pattern Clinic II: Detached DOM, Caches & Globals
points: Leak #4 — detached DOM: a node removed from the document but still referenced from JS keeps its whole subtree in memory
Sources of detached refs: node arrays, template caching, tab keep-alive, storing an element in a module-level variable
Leak #5 — implicit globals: assigning x = 1 without declaration in sloppy mode creates a window property that lives forever
Prevention: 'use strict' / ES modules make accidental globals a hard error
Leak #6 — unbounded caches: a Map used as a memo table grows monotonically — no eviction means no GC
Fix pattern: cap with LRU (Map + delete/re-set for recency) or add TTL/size limits to every cache you write
Module-level log arrays ('just keep the last events') are unbounded in practice — use a ring buffer instead
Detached iframes: holding an object from a removed iframe pins its entire window/world
DevTools retains values you console.log while it's open — noisy dev logging can distort memory readings
Framework variant: refs and state holding nodes/data after unmount, effects registered without cleanup functions
Detection smell: heap snapshot full of 'Detached <div>' entries whose retainer chain ends at one array
Hygiene: null out references in teardown; use WeakMap for any per-node metadata you attach

chapters.title: WeakMap: Attach Without Owning
points: WeakMap definition: a map whose keys are held weakly — an entry exists only while its key is otherwise reachable
Ephemeron model: when the key is collected, the entry (key AND value) becomes collectable — value lifetime is tied to key lifetime
Keys must be objects (registered Symbols allowed in newer spec); primitives throw TypeError
Deliberately unobservable: no iteration, no .size, no keys()/values()/entries() — enumeration would depend on GC timing
Full API: set(k, v), get(k), has(k), delete(k) — that's it
Primary use: attaching metadata to objects you don't own — DOM nodes, library instances — without mutating or pinning them
Other uses: object-keyed memoization/caches that self-clean, per-instance private-ish state
It is not a 'smaller Map': string/number keys need Map; WeakMap is about lifetime, not size
Values are still strong: an entry's value can be a huge object graph — only the key link is weak
Missing keys return undefined silently, and entries can vanish at any GC — write code that tolerates disappearance
Example: WeakMap for node → config object, vs el.dataset for visible strings — WeakMap holds objects, dataset holds strings
Comparison row: Map = strong keys, iterable, sizeable, predictable; WeakMap = weak keys, opaque, GC-coupled

chapters.title: WeakSet, WeakRef & FinalizationRegistry
points: WeakSet: weakly-held membership — add/has/delete only, no iteration or size; entries exist while the object is otherwise reachable
Use case: marking objects as seen/processed/frozen without keeping them alive
WeakRef: new WeakRef(target) holds a weak pointer; ref.deref() returns the target or undefined if it was collected
deref() === undefined is a normal, expected path — every deref call needs a rebuild/degrade branch
WeakRef never keeps its target alive; it only lets you use the object if it happens to still exist
Spec guidance: don't build correctness on weak refs — treat them as an optimization, never the source of truth
FinalizationRegistry: register(target, callback, token) — the callback runs (eventually) after the target is collected
Finalizer timing is unpredictable and may never run before exit — never put essential cleanup there; close files and release handles eagerly
Use unregister(token) inside the callback to drop registry bookkeeping; keep callbacks trivial
Realistic use: libraries doing native/handle interop or cache hygiene — app code rarely needs these
Testing gotcha: WeakRef behavior depends on GC having run — force gc() with --expose-gc in tests
Code sketch: WeakRef-backed view cache — deref, fall back to rebuilding when undefined

chapters.title: Weak vs Strong: Choosing the Right Structure
points: The decision question: 'should this data die when the key dies?' Yes → weak structure; No → Map/Set
Map vs WeakMap: Map has any key type + iteration + size but pins keys; WeakMap trades features for lifetime coupling
Set vs WeakSet mirrors it: enumerability vs non-pinning membership
Cost model: weak structures are not faster or smaller — you pay with lost introspection to gain automatic cleanup
Strong + bounded beats weak + unbounded: an LRU Map with eviction is the right cache when you control the eviction policy
Weak structures shine when key lifetime is owned elsewhere: metadata on DOM nodes, parsed data cached per object
WeakMap vs expando (obj._meta = x): expando is visible, enumerable and strong; WeakMap is invisible and weak — pick by whether others must see it
Private state: WeakMap keyed by instance was the pre-class-fields idiom; real #private fields are now the default answer
Pitfall: using weak refs for correctness (assuming the object 'must still be there') — different GC timings across engines break you
Pitfall: a WeakMap of huge values still eats memory if its keys live long — weak ≠ no memory, just deferred
Migration pattern: convert a leaking Map cache to WeakMap only if entries are per-object and GC-evictable; otherwise add LRU
Summary table: lifetime control, iteration, key types, best use-cases across Map/WeakMap/Set/WeakSet

chapters.title: Debugging with Heap Snapshots
points: Tooling: Chrome DevTools → Memory panel; three modes — Heap snapshot, Allocation instrumentation on timeline, Allocation sampling
Heap snapshot = full point-in-time object graph; leaks show up as growth between snapshots
Three-snapshot technique: baseline → perform the suspected leaking action → snapshot → repeat → snapshot; compare object-count deltas
Shallow size = the object itself; Retained size = object + everything only it keeps alive — sort by retained to find the real holders
Retainers pane: shows the exact chain of references from a root to the object — the fix is always breaking one link in that chain
Filter by constructor: 'Detached' for orphaned DOM, plus search by suspected class/function name
Views: Summary (by constructor), Comparison (snapshot vs snapshot), Containment (heap top-down), Statistics
Allocation instrumentation: blue bars = allocated and still live; gray = already collected — surviving blue bars point at leak sites
Allocation sampling: low-overhead stack sampling — the best first tool when the page slows but you don't know where allocations come from
Force GC before snapshots (trash-can icon or --expose-gc) so dead objects don't pollute the comparison
Node.js: --inspect + Chrome DevTools, process.memoryUsage() heapUsed trend, v8.getHeapSnapshot() for CI diffs
Workflow: reproduce → baseline snapshot → interact → compare → read retainer chain → fix → re-snapshot to verify

chapters.title: Summary: The Leak-Hunter's Checklist
points: The one mental model to keep: reachability from roots decides lifetime; GC is mark-sweep over that graph
Allocate less, don't 'GC harder' — the cheapest memory to collect is memory never allocated
Every subscription gets a symmetric teardown: setInterval↔clearInterval, addEventListener↔removeEventListener or AbortController
Attach, don't own: WeakMap/WeakSet for metadata and membership that should die with the object
WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry are observability and cleanup-hygiene tools — never load-bearing lifecycle logic
Any cache you write needs an eviction story: LRU, TTL or size cap — a Map without limits is a future leak
Avoid accidental globals: strict mode/modules, and null out module-level refs during teardown
Read retained size, not shallow size, when hunting leaks; follow the retainer chain to the one link to break
Make snapshotting a habit: before/after adding intervals, listeners or caches — compare, don't guess
Red flags: heapUsed that ratchets up and never falls, interaction jank from GC, 'Detached' nodes in snapshots
Boiled-down rule: a leak is a reference you forgot you were holding — find the edge, cut the edge
Go deeper: V8 blog's GC deep-dives (Orinoco), MDN Memory Management, TC39 WeakRef proposal explainer
